name: Chakravāla
sub: the wheel that solves x² − Ny² = 1
description: Jayadeva and Bhāskara II's cyclic method for Pell's equation, run live with exact integers.
aria: A spiral wheel of light where each spoke is one turn of the chakravala method
intro: Find whole numbers with x² − 61y² = 1. The smallest answer has ten digits. In 1150 Bhāskara II found it with a wheel of steps that always comes back to 1.

tutorial.b: Find whole numbers with x² − 61y² = 1. The smallest answer has x = 1,766,319,049.
The method keeps a² − 61b² = k, where k measures how far off it is. It starts at 8² − 61 = 3, so k = 3.
Each stop on the wheel is one turn of the method. Its label shows the new k.
This line checks the equation with the real numbers after every turn. When k reaches 1 the puzzle is solved.
Pick another N here. For 991 the answer has 30 digits, and the wheel still finds it.

sound:
You hear k. Each turn plucks a note whose pitch is set by how big k is: about log₂|k| steps up the scale. Big near-misses sound high and small ones low, so as the wheel homes in, the melody settles down.

When k = 1 two bowls ring together, on Sa and an octave and a fifth above (× 3): the equation is solved.

Every chamber plays in Raag Bhupali: five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as whole-number ratios of the home note Sa (138.6 Hz here): 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3. Simple ratios mean the sound waves line up every few cycles, so they never clash. That lets the math pick any note it likes and it still sounds like music. Underneath, a tanpura drone holds Sa and Pa, and a bansuri improvises in the same raag. The santoor and the singing bowl are the ones the math plays.

faq.a: x² − N·y² = 1 in whole numbers, for N not a perfect square. Indian mathematicians called it vargaprakṛti. Europe named it after Pell by mistake.
k = a² − N·b², how far the current pair (a, b) is from solving the equation. The wheel ends when k = 1.
m must make k divide a + b·m, and among those, m² should be as close to N as possible. That keeps the next k small.
Brahmagupta's composition rule (628 CE): combine two solutions of x² − Ny² = k into a solution for the product of their k's. Each turn uses it, then divides by k².
In 1657 Fermat challenged European mathematicians with N = 61. Bhāskara II's Bījagaṇita had the answer around 1150.
For N = 61 this plain version takes 13 turns. Selenius (1975) showed the chakravāla is a shortest-possible continued-fraction method.
Bhupali uses five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as the ratios 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2 and 5/3. It has no half-steps, so any note the math picks sounds consonant against the drone.

Sa is 138.6 Hz. Every other note is Sa times a whole-number ratio (9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3) or that times a power of 2 for higher octaves. Which note plays is chosen by a number in the scene. Open 'why this sound' to watch it live.
The haze behind the math is a kaleidoscope shader. Its symmetry follows the chamber's math, but it's decoration. Say 'glow 0' to switch it off and see only the math.
Isha Maini, a data science student at Emory. Each chamber's math is written and tested in Python and JavaScript before it's drawn.
